## 1. Bio-inspired backpropagation-free training for optical neural networks

- Venue: Light Science & Applications, 2026
- Score: 0.88
- Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41377-026-02394-3

### Core problem

Traditional optical neural networks (T-ONNs) rely on error backpropagation, which is incompatible with physical optical systems due to the lack of reciprocal error paths and extreme sensitivity to fabrication imperfections.

### Method and architecture

The proposed bio-inspired backpropagation-free optical neural network (B-ONN) uses a layer-wise target propagation mechanism. Trainable error convolution kernels enable each layer to perform local learning based on target signals instead of chain-ruled gradients, eliminating the need for precise optical conjugation between forward and backward paths.

### Main contributions

- A backpropagation-free training method for optical neural networks using target propagation with trainable error convolution kernels.
- Demonstrated comparable accuracy to traditional ONN on MNIST (93.25%) and Fashion-MNIST (82.28%).
- Superior robustness against phase noise (75% accuracy at σ ≈ 0.4π) and alignment errors (75% accuracy within ±3 pixels).
- Physical validation on a programmable SLM system achieving 95% handwritten digit recognition accuracy.
- Chip-scale integration via nano printing with 94% accuracy, confirming transferability to fixed devices.
- Inherent structural robustness from smooth learned phase distributions without noise-augmented training.

### Reported results

- B-ONN achieves 93.25% accuracy on MNIST. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- B-ONN achieves 82.28% accuracy on Fashion-MNIST. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- B-ONN achieves 75% accuracy under phase noise of σ ≈ 0.4π. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- B-ONN achieves 75% accuracy within alignment errors of ±3 pixels. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- Physical SLM validation achieved 95% accuracy in handwritten digit recognition. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- Chip-scale integration via nano printing maintained 94% accuracy. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)

### Research value

The approach addresses a fundamental incompatibility in training physical ONNs, potentially enabling practical deployment of robust, energy-efficient optical computing in real-world applications.

### Limitations and open questions

- The abstract does not discuss scalability to deeper architectures beyond those tested.
- Performance on more complex datasets or tasks is not mentioned.
- Comparison to other backpropagation-free optical training methods is not provided.
- The impact of fabrication imperfections in chip-scale integration on long-term stability is not detailed.

## 2. 65 TOPS optoelectronic multi-core computing unlocking multi-feature fusion enhancement

- Venue: Nature Communications, 2026
- Score: 0.85
- Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76128-9

### Core problem

Current optical computing implementations suffer from speed limitations and multi-core integration challenges, hindering scalable, energy-efficient AI hardware.

### Method and architecture

A high-throughput optical processing unit (OPU) exploiting coherent interference, wavelength-division multiplexing, and spatial parallelism. Four optical analog cores are integrated on a monolithic chip to support 124-channel parallel processing. An optoelectronic convolutional neural network (OE-CNN) is constructed, fusing the OPU's parallel 4-kernel convolution and average pooling operations with electronic nonlinear activation and fully connected operations.

### Main contributions

- Demonstration of a monolithic chip with four integrated optical analog cores that simultaneously exploit coherent interference, WDM, and spatial parallelism.
- Achieving 65.04 TOPS computational speed and 5.16 TOPS/mm2 compute density through 124-channel parallel task processing.
- Construction of an OE-CNN that combines optical 4‑kernel parallel convolution and average pooling with electronic nonlinear activation for multi‑feature fusion.
- MNIST classification accuracy of 95.08%, a 9.20% improvement over the single‑core counterpart, attributed to multi‑feature fusion via parallel convolution.

### Reported results

- The OPU achieves 65.04 trillion operations per second (TOPS) computational speed. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- The OPU achieves 5.16 TOPS/mm2 compute density. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- The OPU supports 124‑channel parallel task processing. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- The OE-CNN achieves 95.08% MNIST classification accuracy, a 9.20% improvement over a single‑core counterpart. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)

### Research value

The demonstration of a scalable multi‑core optical processing unit that achieves high throughput (65 TOPS) and high compute density (5.16 TOPS/mm2) addresses critical bottlenecks in optical AI accelerators. The multi‑feature fusion OE‑CNN illustrates a practical architecture for leveraging optical parallelism to enhance classification accuracy, potentially paving the way for many‑core optoelectronic intelligent computing systems.

### Limitations and open questions

- The evaluation is limited to the MNIST dataset; performance on more complex benchmarks is not reported.
- Details on energy efficiency, latency, and comparison to state‑of‑the‑art electronic accelerators are absent.
- The abstract does not discuss scalability limits, fabrication yield, or crosstalk in the multi‑core monolithic integration.
- Long‑term stability, environmental sensitivity, and reconfigurability of the optical cores are not addressed.
- The role and implementation of electronic nonlinear activation and fully connected layers are not described.

## 3. All-optical computing towards 100-GHz clock rates

- Venue: Light Science & Applications, 2026
- Score: 0.85
- Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41377-026-02314-5

### Core problem

Conventional electronic processors have stagnated at ~5 GHz clock rates for nearly two decades, limiting real-time processing and control of ultrafast information systems.

### Method and architecture

All-optical recurrent neural network that performs linear operations, nonlinear functions, and memory entirely in the optical domain, leveraging ultrafast optical characteristics while circumventing electronic bottlenecks.

### Main contributions

- Proposes and experimentally demonstrates an all-optical recurrent neural network for computing beyond electronic clock rate limits.
- Achieves accuracy surpassing a purely linear model up to 80 GHz clock rates depending on the task.
- Demonstrates noisy waveform classification and ultrafast in-situ analysis of soliton states from integrated optical microresonators.
- Illustrates application for generative AI using quantum fluctuations to generate images without input optical signals.

### Reported results

- All-optical computer realizes linear operations, nonlinear functions, and memory entirely in the optical domain with accuracy surpassing a purely linear model up to 80 GHz clock rates depending on the task. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- Experimentally demonstrated a prototypical task of noisy waveform classification. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- Performed ultrafast in-situ analysis of the soliton states from integrated optical microresonators. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)
- Illustrated the application of the architecture for generative artificial intelligence based on quantum fluctuations to generate images even in the absence of input optical signals. (`reported_by_authors`, basis: abstract)

### Research value

Highlights the potential of all-optical computing to surpass digital electronics by utilizing ultrafast linear, nonlinear, and memory functions and quantum fluctuations, enabling applications requiring real-time processing of ultrafast information systems.

### Limitations and open questions

- Performance and accuracy only demonstrated up to 80 GHz; generalization to higher rates and other tasks not shown.
- Scalability and practical implementation challenges of all-optical systems not addressed.
- Comparison to state-of-the-art electronic or hybrid approaches not provided.
- Long-term stability and robustness of all-optical memory and nonlinear functions not discussed.
- Energy efficiency and footprint relative to electronic alternatives not analyzed.
